In [[category theory]], an '''allegory''' is a [[category (mathematics)|category]] that has some of the structure of the category '''Rel''' of [[Set (mathematics)|sets]] and [[binary relation]]s between them. Allegories can be used as an abstraction of categories of relations, and in this sense the theory of allegories is a generalization of [[relation algebra]] to relations between different sorts. Allegories are also useful in defining and investigating certain constructions in category theory, such as [[regular category|exact]] completions.

==Definition==

An allegory is a [[Category (mathematics)|category]] in which
* every morphism <math>R : X\to Y</math> is associated with an '''anti-involution''', i.e. a morphism <math>R^\circ : Y\to X</math> with <math>R^{\circ\circ} = R</math> and <math>(RS)^\circ = S^\circ R^\circ\text{;}</math> and
* every pair of morphisms <math>R,S : X\to Y</math> with common domain/codomain is associated with an '''intersection''', i.e. a morphism <math>R \cap S : X\to Y</math>
all such that
* intersections are [[idempotent]]: <math>R\cap R = R,</math> [[commutative]]: <math>R\cap S = S\cap R,</math> and [[associative]]: <math>(R\cap S)\cap T = R\cap (S\cap T);</math>
* anti-involution [[Distributive property|distributes]] over intersection: <math>(R\cap S)^\circ = R^\circ \cap S^\circ;</math>
* composition is semi-distributive over intersection: <math>R(S\cap T) \subseteq RS\cap RT</math> and <math>(R\cap S)T \subseteq RT\cap ST;</math> and
* the modularity law is satisfied: <math>RS \cap T \subseteq (R\cap TS^\circ)S.</math>
Here, the order defined by the intersection <math>R \subseteq S</math> is used as an abbreviation of <math>R = R\cap S.</math>

A first example of an allegory is the [[Category of relations|category of sets and relations]]. The [[Object (category theory)|objects]] of this allegory are sets, and a morphism <math>X \to Y</math> is a binary relation between <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math>. Composition of morphisms is [[composition of relations]], and the anti-involution of <math>R</math> is the [[converse relation]] <math>R^\circ</math>; we have <math>y R^\circ x</math> if and only if <math>xRy</math>. Intersection of morphisms is (set-theoretic) [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of relations.

==Regular categories and allegories==

===Allegories of relations in regular categories===

In a category <math>C</math>, a '''relation''' between objects <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> is a [[span (category theory)|span]] of morphisms <math>X\gets R\to Y</math> that is jointly [[Monomorphism|monic]]. Two such spans <math>X\gets S\to Y</math> and <math>X\gets T\to Y</math> are considered equivalent when there is an isomorphism between <math>S</math> and <math>T</math> that make everything commute; strictly speaking, relations are only defined up to equivalence (one may formalise this either by using [[equivalence class]]es or by using [[Bicategory|bicategories]]). If the category <math>C</math> has products, a relation between <math>X</math> and <math>Y</math> is the same thing as a [[monomorphism]] into <math>X\times Y</math> (or an equivalence class of such). In the presence of [[Pullback (category theory)|pullbacks]] and a proper [[factorization system]], one can define the composition of relations. The composition <math>X\gets R\to Y\gets S\to Z</math> is found by first pulling back the cospan <math>R\to Y\gets S</math> and then taking the jointly-monic image of the resulting span <math>X\gets R\gets\bullet\to S\to Z</math>.

Composition of relations will be associative if the factorization system is appropriately stable. In this case, one can consider a category {{math|Rel(''C'')}}, with the same objects as <math>C</math>, but where morphisms are relations between the objects. The identity relations are the diagonals <math>X \to X\times X.</math>

A [[regular category]] (a category with finite limits and images in which covers are stable under pullback) has a stable regular epi/mono factorization system. The category of relations for a regular category is always an allegory. Anti-involution is defined by turning the source/target of the relation around, and intersections are intersections of [[subobject]]s, computed by pullback.

===Maps in allegories, and tabulations===

A morphism <math>R</math> in an allegory <math>A</math> is called a '''map''' if it is entire <math>(1\subseteq R^\circ R)</math> and deterministic <math>(RR^\circ \subseteq 1).</math> Another way of saying this is that a map is a morphism that has a [[adjoint functor|right adjoint]] in <math>A</math> when <math>A</math> is considered, using the local order structure, as a [[2-category]]. Maps in an allegory are closed under identity and composition. Thus, there is a [[subcategory]] {{math|Map(''A'')}} of <math>A</math> with the same objects but only the maps as morphisms. For a regular category <math>C</math>, there is an isomorphism of categories <math>C \cong \operatorname{Map}(\operatorname{Rel}(C)).</math> In particular, a morphism in {{math|Map(Rel('''Set'''))}} is just an ordinary [[Function (mathematics)|set function]].

In an allegory, a morphism <math>R : X\to Y</math> is '''tabulated''' by a pair of maps <math>f : Z\to X</math> and <math>g : Z\to Y</math> if <math>gf^\circ = R</math> and <math>f^\circ f \cap g^\circ g = 1</math>. An allegory is called '''tabular''' if every morphism has a tabulation. For a regular category <math>C</math>, the allegory {{math|Rel(''C'')}} is always tabular. On the other hand, for any tabular allegory <math>A</math>, the category {{math|Map(''A'')}} of maps is a locally regular category: it has pullbacks, [[Equalizer (mathematics)|equalizers]], and images that are stable under pullback. This is enough to study relations in {{math|Map(''A'')}}, and in this setting, <math>A\cong \operatorname{Rel}(\operatorname{Map}(A)).</math>

===Unital allegories and regular categories of maps===

A '''unit''' in an allegory is an object <math>U</math> for which the identity is the largest morphism <math>U\to U</math>, and such that from every other object, there is an entire relation to <math>U</math>. An allegory with a unit is called '''unital'''. Given a tabular allegory <math>A</math>, the category {{math|Map(''A'')}} is a regular category (it has a [[terminal object]]) if and only if <math>A</math> is unital.

===More sophisticated kinds of allegory===
Additional properties of allegories can be axiomatized. '''Distributive allegories''' have a [[Union (set theory)|union]]-like operation that is suitably well-behaved, and '''division allegories''' have a generalization of the division operation of [[relation algebra]]. '''Power allegories''' are distributive division allegories with additional [[powerset]]-like structure. The connection between allegories and regular categories can be developed into a connection between power allegories and [[toposes]].
